title: Mosaic handoff allocator - token/request hybrid fairness notes
body:
Purpose
This is a working note to capture the Mosaic Handoff Allocator idea: a hybrid continuous-batching scheduler that explicitly separates token coalescing from request-level fairness while minimizing KV cache churn and enabling kernel-aware packing. Goal is practical heuristics and an ops-friendly set of knobs we can test on staging clusters.

Summary of idea
- Continuous token coalescing stays as our low-latency path: requests stream tokens into per-worker micro-windows that aim to fill GPU batches without incurring long request delays.
- A lightweight allocator (the Mosaic Handoff) runs per-worker and decides when to flush a micro-window to the kernel, but can also hand off partial token sequences to an offload queue to preserve fairness across requests/clients.
- Fairness is enforced at two layers: (1) soft request-level credits ensure no client monopolizes window occupancy, (2) token-level admission and pacing maximize kernel utilization.
- KV cache affinity is first-class: when handing off or merging token groups across workers, the allocator prefers merges that maintain or restore local KV cache hits to avoid full KV replication.

Motivation / problem statement
- Pure token-level continuous batching squeezes GPU utilization but can starve small/latency-sensitive requests and cause cross-shard KV thrash when groups are merged incorrectly.
- Pure request-level batching preserves fairness but underutilizes GPUs when request length distributions are spiky and arrivals are bursty.
- Previous sketches (microwindow, sliding-window) do not explicitly consider kernel packing constraints for quantized/packed kernels; naive merges produce shapes that run poorly on certain kernels.

Design goals and constraints
- Latency SLOs: 95th percentile tail should remain within current SLO for latency-sensitive routes; configurable per-route latency budgets.
- Throughput: preserve or improve tokens/sec compared to current continuous coalescer baseline for mixed workloads.
- Fairness: per-client and per-route starvation protection; fairness knobs should be auditable and adjustable.
- KV churn: minimize KV cache misses caused by merging shards/worker reassignments.
- Kernel-aware packing: prefer kernels with good perf for given sequence-length distribution; optionally avoid packing shapes that trigger slow kernels.

High-level components
1) Admission controller (Front-end):
   - Tracks per-client credits (decay window), per-route budgets, and request priority class.
   - Assigns tokens to worker micro-windows using a best-effort affinity (client -> preferred-worker map).
   - Emits an admission token that includes: request-id, client-id, current-client-credit, kv-shard-hint.
2) Worker micro-window manager (Mosaic tile):
   - Maintains multiple tiles (micro-windows) concurrently; a tile is a contiguous set of tokens from several requests.
   - Tiles have metadata: expected kernel-shape, kv-affinity-score (how many tokens reference local KV pages), aggregate-client-credit, earliest-deadline.
   - Tile flush triggers: time threshold, kernel-shape hit, credit depletion, or explicit fairness preemption.
3) Handoff allocator (local, per-node):
   - If a tile is not flushable without violating fairness, the allocator may split the tile and hand off the tail to an offload queue.
   - Offload queue entries carry KV delta pointers instead of full KV to keep memory cheap; offloaded tails are later reassembled with best-effort affinity.
   - Offload policy aims to maximize: local-kv-affinity * kernel-efficiency - fairness-penalty.
4) Offload merge engine (global-ish):
   - Periodically consumes offload queue and tries to reconstruct kernel-friendly batches by matching kv-affinity hints and kernel-shape targets.
   - Uses a cheap bin-packing heuristic: group tails by target shape and kv-affinity; prefer merges within same rack/zone.

Kernel-aware heuristics
- Maintain a small SLO-like table per-model: {shape -> median-ms, 90p-ms, kernel-id}. The allocator prefers shapes with good median/90p and will avoid producing a batch shape that maps to kernel-id X if 90p of X is > threshold.
- When possible, break or pad tiles to a shape known to run well on the selected kernel (e.g., pad short sequences to a 16-token alignment for an optimized kernel). Padding should be limited and charged to the request but counted in telemetry.

KV cache affinity
- Each token carries a KV keyset fingerprint; workers maintain a sliding LRU of hot keysets.
- Tiles track the fraction of tokens whose keyset is local. The allocator scores merges with a simple logistic function: score = 2*local_fraction + 1.5*kernel_score - 3*fairness_violation_risk.
- Offload entries attempt to annotate thin diffs (keys that are not in the local LRU) to avoid full copy on merge. When diff is large, prefer to route that entry to the worker that already holds the majority of keys.

Fairness model
- Per-client credit windows: each client accrues credits proportional to time since last served and decays while being served; admission requires non-negative credits or explicit priority.
- Latency budget enforcement: requests have a deadline derived from route config; when approaching deadline, any tile containing an about-to-expire request gets preemptive flush (even if kernel shape is suboptimal).
- Controlled inversion: in overload scenarios we allow temporarily lowering kernel-efficiency to serve higher-priority/latency requests — this is tracked as "fairness debt" and used to bias future merges toward higher efficiency.

Telemetry and ops knobs
- Emit events: tile_created, tile_flushed, tile_split, offload_created, offload_merged with attached scalar tags (kv-local-fraction, kernel-shape, aggregate-client-credit, flush-latency).
- Runtime knobs (per-cluster and per-route): max_tile_age_ms, min_kernel_shape_util, kv_affinity_threshold, client_credit_decay_ms, allow_padding.
- A daily job recomputes kernel shape table for models based on recent perf sampling traces.

Experiment plan (staging)
1) Canary A: enable Mosaic allocator for a low-traffic compute node group and route a non-critical route. Measure tokens/sec, 95th/99th latency, KV miss rate.
2) Canary B: same as A but with kernel-aware heuristics disabled to isolate benefit of kernel packing.
3) Fairness stress test: synthetic clients with skewed request sizes to evaluate starvation metrics and fairness debt accrual/repayment.
4) KV-affinity test: instrument hotset movements and measure offload-induced KV replications.

Open questions / trade-offs
- Complexity vs. benefit: are offload queues and diffs worth the added scheduling complexity? Could a simpler per-shard pinning plus conservative merging achieve most benefits?
- Billing and observable charge for padding and offload overheads: ops need clear accounting so customers are not surprised by extra tokens due to padding/merging.
- Interactions with Dedicated/Private: in private deployments we cannot rely on cross-node merges across air-gapped zones — so policy must be configurable to disallow remote merges.
- How to gracefully fallback when kernel table is stale or mispredicts the slow kernel? Conservative approach: prefer shape that was safe historically; optimistic approach: try new shapes and roll back if latency regresses.

Rough pseudocode (allocator loop)
for each worker tick:
  accept incoming tokens to preferred tiles
  for tile in tiles:
    if tile.age > max_tile_age_ms or tile.deadline_soon():
      flush(tile)
    else if tile.kernel_shape in preferred_shapes and tile.kv_affinity >= kv_affinity_threshold:
      flush(tile)
    else if tile.aggregate_client_credit < negative_threshold:
      split = tile.split_by_credit();
      handoff(split.tail)

handoff(tail):
  create offload_entry with kv_diff = compute_kv_diff(tail)
  push to offload_queue

merge_offload_queue():
  group = binpack_by_shape_and_kv_hint(offload_queue)
  for group_item in group:
    if group_item.locality_ok():
      assemble_and_flush(group_item)

Next steps / TODOs
- Implement telemetry hooks and minimal kernel shape table in serving-runtime branch.
- Prototype offload queue with simplified kv-diff (list of hot keys) and eviction policy.
- Run A/B on staging for 2 weeks: baseline vs mosaic allocator with kernel-aware heuristics on.
- Product: discuss per-route knobs for allowing padding and offload in hosted API docs.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally exploratory; looking for pushback on complexity and on the fairness accounting model. Concrete questions:
  * Is per-client credit the right primitive or should we operate per-customer (multi-API-key)?
  * How aggressive should the allocator be in padding to favor kernel shapes?
  * Are we comfortable with offloading partial tails across nodes in Dedicated/Private deployments?

References / related tickets
- RUN-732: prototype mosaic allocator (Linear)
- PR 1283: initial wire types for tile/offload entries in runtime repo
- perf/kv-hotset-analysis/2024-12: internal perf notebook (link in PR)

End of note.
